title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
authors: Pakmanee N, Limitlaohaphan C, Saengpetch N, Kijkunasathian C, Lertbutsayanukul C, Wanitchanont T, Thamyongkit S, Fuangfa P, Vijittrakarnrung C
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 13. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70685.
Online  ahead of print.

Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated 
meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.

Pakmanee N(1)(2), Limitlaohaphan C(1), Saengpetch N(1), Kijkunasathian C(1), 
Lertbutsayanukul C(1), Wanitchanont T(3), Thamyongkit S(3), Fuangfa P(4), 
Vijittrakarnrung C(1).



PURPOSE: To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on 
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic 
meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in 
isolated meniscal tears.
METHODS: In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled 
trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI 
were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, 
lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the 
International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. 
Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities 
Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a 
visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse 
events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, 
two-blinded assessors).
RESULTS: Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were 
randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the 
augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; 
p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, 
Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 
months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC 
score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), 
Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, 
IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 
7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; 
unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications 
occurred within 12 months.
CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior 
patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an 
increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between 
groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS 
augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and 
structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and 
indications of BMS.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.

title: Success of debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention for acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Esmaeili S, Razzaghof M, Ayati Firoozabadi M, Mortazavi SMJ
abstract:
1. J Bone Jt Infect. 2026 Nov 9;11(6):673-686. doi: 10.5194/jbji-11-673-2026. 
eCollection 2026.

Success of debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention for acute 
hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection: a systematic review and 
meta-analysis.

Esmaeili S(1)(2), Razzaghof M(1)(2), Ayati Firoozabadi M(1)(2), Mortazavi 
SMJ(1)(2).



Background: Acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection after hip or knee 
arthroplasty is difficult to treat. The method of debridement, antibiotics, and 
implant retention (DAIR) is widely used, but reported success rates vary, and 
predictors of failure remain unclear. Methods: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web 
of Science, and Embase from inception through 26 November 2025 for studies 
reporting outcomes of DAIR in acute hematogenous periprosthetic joint infection. 
Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed 
methodological quality using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. The primary outcome 
was pooled treatment success. Results: Forty-nine studies were included in the 
qualitative synthesis. Reported success rates ranged from 20 % to 100 %, with a 
pooled success rate of 64.5 % (95 % confidence interval, 59.3 %-69.4 %; I2 = 72 
%, τ2 = 0.44 ) in the meta-analysis. This pooled estimate describes an average 
across heterogeneous cohorts and should not be used as a patient-specific 
prediction. Success was higher in total hip arthroplasty than in total knee 
arthroplasty (69.4 % vs. 63.2 %). Outcomes improved over time, from 44.9 % 
before 2010 to 68.7 % in 2020-2025. Staphylococcus aureus infection and 
prolonged symptom duration before debridement were the most consistently 
reported predictors of treatment failure, whereas some included studies reported 
improved outcomes with modular component exchange. Conclusion: DAIR controls 
infection in about two-thirds of patients with acute hematogenous periprosthetic 
joint infection. Failure remains common, especially with S. aureus infection or 
delayed intervention, supporting early diagnosis, prompt surgery, and careful 
patient selection.

title: Facility Cost Differences Between Single-stage and Two-stage Exchange for Chronic Periprosthetic Joint Infection: A Time-driven Activity-based Costing Analysis.
authors: Lam AD, Sutton RM, Lizcano JD, Sherman MB, Brown S, Courtney PM, Krueger CA
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3305-e3311. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01024. Epub 2026 Jun 18.

Facility Cost Differences Between Single-stage and Two-stage Exchange for 
Chronic Periprosthetic Joint Infection: A Time-driven Activity-based Costing 
Analysis.

Lam AD(1), Sutton RM, Lizcano JD, Sherman MB, Brown S, Courtney PM, Krueger CA.



BACKGROUND: With increasing data supporting the use of single-stage exchange 
over two-stage exchange for select patients with periprosthetic joint infection 
(PJI) after total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA), it 
is important to specifically quantify cost differences between the two 
procedures. This study aimed to compare itemized facility costs of single-stage 
and two-stage exchange.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study identified 118 consecutive patients who 
were diagnosed with chronic PJI and underwent revision THA or TKA at a single 
high-volume academic institution. Of 63 hip PJI patients (53.4%), 38 (60.3%) 
underwent single-stage revision and 25 (39.7%) underwent two-stage revision. 
From 55 knee PJI patients (46.6%), 19 (34.5%) underwent single-stage revision 
and 36 (65.5%) underwent two-stage exchange. Patients were excluded if they had 
soft-tissue coverage requirements or extensive bone loss requiring 
endoprosthesis. Facility costs were calculated using time-driven activity-based 
costing methodology. Costs were combined for the two hospital admissions for a 
two-stage exchange.
RESULTS: Patients undergoing single-stage revision TKA had lower personnel 
($46,397 vs. $78,765, P < 0.001), implant ($19,822 vs. $85,605, P < 0.001), and 
overall costs ($79,548 vs. $171,592, P < 0.001) when compared with two-stage 
revision. Similarly, patients undergoing single-stage revision THA had lower 
personnel ($46,718 vs. 99,255, P < 0.001), implant ($19,936 vs. 73,372, P < 
0.001), and overall costs ($79,349 vs. 187,251, P < 0.001) than two-staged 
procedures. Implant costs demonstrated the highest variation between two-stage 
and one-stage revisions for TKA (4.3 times) and THA (3.7 times). Total surgical 
time was significantly longer in two-staged THA (365 vs. 175 minutes, P < 0.001) 
and TKA (256 vs. 162 minutes, P < 0.001) revisions.
CONCLUSION: Single-staged revisions cost markedly less than two-staged 
procedures for first-time, chronic PJI when using strict surgical indications. 
Given the growing emphasis on value-based care, if single-stage arthroplasty is 
at least as effective as two-stage exchange in some PJI settings, the cost 
savings of this procedure would be tremendous.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Clinical outcomes of revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with and without a lateral extra-articular procedure: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Wang H, Xu L, Wang B, Xiang X, Xia D, Gong J
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Nov 13;21:101241. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101241. Online
ahead  of print.

Clinical outcomes of revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with and 
without a lateral extra-articular procedure: A systematic review and 
meta-analysis.

Wang H(1), Xu L(1), Wang B(1), Xiang X(1), Xia D(1), Gong J(2).



IMPORTANCE: Revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (R-ACLR) has less 
favorable outcomes than primary reconstruction. Earlier revision-specific 
meta-analyses included eight and ten comparative studies. The clinical value of 
adding a lateral extra-articular procedure (LEAP) remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to compare clinical outcomes after R-ACLR performed 
with versus without LEAP augmentation.
EVIDENCE REVIEW: PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 
1, 2006, to April 30, 2026. Comparative studies reporting clinical follow-up of 
at least 24 months were eligible; the randomized trial also supplied objective 
stability measurements at 1 year. Random-effects meta-analyses evaluated 
function, stability, failure or rerevision, and return to activity. 
Methodological quality and certainty were assessed using the Downs and Black 
checklist and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and 
Evaluation framework.
FINDINGS: Fourteen studies included 1134 patients (559 with LEAP and 575 with 
isolated R-ACLR). The failure analysis included 11 studies and 1023 patients: 
29/517 versus 69/506 events (risk ratio [RR], 0.44; 95% confidence interval 
[CI], 0.29-0.68; P < 0.001; I2 = 3.9%). Certainty in this combined estimate was 
very low. LEAP augmentation was associated with less anterior laxity (Hedges' g, 
0.46; 95% CI, 0.21-0.71) and fewer positive pivot shifts (RR, 0.51; 95% CI, 
0.30-0.87). The subjective International Knee Documentation Committee score 
difference was small (mean difference, 2.91; 95% CI, 0.23-5.59). Return to any 
sport was informed by only two studies and 87 patients (RR, 1.10; 95% CI, 
0.92-1.32; P = 0.278).
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: LEAP augmentation was associated with lower observed 
failure or rerevision risk and greater postoperative stability. Patient-reported 
differences were small and inconsistent. Predominantly nonrandomized evidence 
and very low certainty in the combined estimates limit causal inference and 
subgroup recommendations.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.
REGISTRATION: International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews, 
CRD420261441628.

title: Meniscus centralization: Are we treating meniscal extrusion as the cause of osteoarthritis or simply its consequence?
authors: Dzidzishvili L, Ostojic M, Chahla J, LaPrade RF
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 11. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70676.
Online  ahead of print.

Meniscus centralization: Are we treating meniscal extrusion as the cause of 
osteoarthritis or simply its consequence?

Dzidzishvili L(1), Ostojic M(2), Chahla J(3), LaPrade RF(4).



Residual meniscal extrusion (ME) is considered an important factor jeopardizing 
the long-term success of otherwise technically successful medial meniscus 
posterior root (MMPR) repair. Biomechanical and clinical studies have shown that 
meniscal centralization can reduce extrusion, restore contact mechanics and 
improve short-term clinical outcomes. However, an important paradox remains: 
many patients with pre-existing osteoarthritis (OA) and persistent ME after MMPR 
repair maintain good clinical outcomes despite continued radiographic 
progression. Although the biomechanical rationale for centralization is 
compelling, its clinical value may be more complex in the middle-aged, 
degenerative knee. Progressive changes in tissue elasticity, capsular 
attenuation and joint biology may contribute to meniscal displacement, 
suggesting that ME may be less a primary driver of degeneration than a 
manifestation of an underlying OA. This raises a fundamental question: Are we 
treating the right target? Is residual ME a modifiable driver of disease 
progression, or does it primarily reflect the natural history of joint 
degeneration? This Editorial critically examines the emerging evidence on 
meniscal centralization, explores the clinical relevance of residual ME and 
highlights key questions that can guide future research.

title: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears in the anterior cruciate ligament-injured knee: Current concepts.
authors: Shirouei S, Ayati Firoozabadi M, Mortazavi SMJ
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Nov 10;21:101243. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101243. Online
ahead  of print.

Lateral meniscus posterior root tears in the anterior cruciate ligament-injured 
knee: Current concepts.

Shirouei S(1), Ayati Firoozabadi M(2), Mortazavi SMJ(3).



Lateral meniscus posterior root tears (LMPRTs) compromise load transmission and 
secondary stability in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-injured knee and may 
be missed on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This narrative current-concepts 
review addresses incidence, risk factors, biomechanics, diagnosis, 
classification, treatment, and outcomes, while distinguishing root tears from 
lateral meniscal oblique radial tears (LMORTs). Primary ACL reconstruction 
(ACLR) cohorts report LMPRT frequencies of 7.1%, 10.0%, and 12.2%; a mixed 
primary/revision cohort reports 6.6% and selected revision cohorts report 20.5% 
and 40.7%. These study-specific estimates differ in lesion definition and 
ascertainment. Contact injury, concomitant medial meniscal pathology, and 
increased lateral posterior tibial slope are recurring associations. Individual 
MRI signs have limited sensitivity; combined assessment and arthroscopic 
inspection and probing support diagnosis. LaPrade et al. describe root-tear 
morphology, Forkel and Petersen additionally consider meniscofemoral ligament 
integrity, and LMORT typing describes posterior-horn oblique radial tears. The 
systems overlap for near-root lesions and are descriptive frameworks rather than 
validated treatment algorithms. Selected stable lesions may be observed; 
repairable unstable lesions are generally treated with footprint fixation or 
side-to-side repair, according to anatomy and tissue quality. Repair with ACLRn 
is associated with improved patient-reported outcomes and high 
complete-or-partial healing proportions in selected series. Clinical improvement 
in ACL graft survivorship has not been demonstrated. Heterogeneous definitions, 
predominantly lower-level evidence, variable rehabilitation, and limited 
long-term comparative data, constrain conclusions about cartilage preservation 
and optimal treatment.

title: Frailty is a Vital Tool for Predicting Outcomes Following Prophylactic Femur Fixation.
authors: Sbaih O, Koltenyuk V, Gupta N, Dixon L, Gill V, Ogburn M, Williamson TK, Alderete J
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3312-e3319. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00647. Epub 2026 Jun 23.

Frailty is a Vital Tool for Predicting Outcomes Following Prophylactic Femur 
Fixation.

Sbaih O(1), Koltenyuk V, Gupta N, Dixon L, Gill V, Ogburn M, Williamson TK, 
Alderete J.



BACKGROUND: Frailty measures have become increasingly common in the literature 
as proposed mechanisms for identifying patients at risk of adverse postoperative 
outcomes. Prophylactic femur fixation in patients with metastatic disease can 
prevent future fracture and improve quality of life; however, these patients are 
inherently high-risk surgical candidates. The role of this study is to 
characterize the relationship between frailty and postoperative outcomes in 
patients undergoing prophylactic femoral fixation (ProphFF) and compare the 
predictive ability of different frailty measures for adverse outcomes in this 
population.
METHODS: Data from the 2015 to 2020 American College of Surgeons National 
Surgical Quality Improvement Program database was used. The study focused on 
patients aged ≥18 years undergoing ProphFF and those undergoing PathFF. Frailty 
was measured using both the revised Risk Analysis Index (RAI-rev) and the 
five-factor modified Frailty Index (mFI-5). Primary outcomes included 30-day 
mortality, major complications, unplanned readmission, and unplanned revision 
surgery, nonhome discharge, and extended length of stay. Propensity score 
matching was employed to adjust for baseline differences of age, body mass 
index, sex, functional status, and ASA between ProphFF and PathFF groups. 
Statistical methods included multivariable logistic regression and receiver 
operating characteristic curve analysis to evaluate the relationships between 
frailty measures and postoperative outcomes.
RESULTS: A total of 921 patients (57.7% female, median age 65 years [IQR, 56 to 
72 years]) undergoing ProphFF or PathFF were included. Multivariable analysis 
demonstrated that increasing frailty increased odds of 30-day mortality, with 
each 1-point increase in RAI-rev and mFI-5 associated with a 5% (OR: 1.05, 95% 
CI, 1.01 to 1.08; P < 0.01) and 31% (OR: 1.31, 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.71; P < 0.05) 
higher mortality risk, respectively. Propensity score matching resulted in 842 
patients (421 prophylactic and 421 pathologic). Patients undergoing PathFF had 
higher likelihood of mortality compared with patients undergoing ProphFF (OR: 
2.79, 95% CI, 1.61 to 4.82; P < 0.01). RAI-rev (C-statistic 0.73 [95% CI, 0.71 
to 0.75]) had superior discrimination for mortality compared with mFI-5 
(C-statistic 0.57 [95% CI, 0.54 to 0.59], P < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Increasing preoperative frailty scores, particularly as measured by 
the revised Risk Analysis Index, were independent predictors of mortality and 
morbidity in patients undergoing prophylactic femur fixation. Pathologic 
fracture fixation demonstrated higher risk of revision surgery and mortality 
compared with prophylactic fixation. These findings suggest that the RAI-rev may 
be a valuable tool for identifying high-risk patients and optimizing surgical 
candidate selection before prophylactic femur fixation, potentially improving 
outcomes in this complex patient population.

title: Impact of an Orthopaedic-Driven Perioperative Protocol to Optimize Social and Medical Risk (SAFE) following Elective Total Joint Arthroplasty in a Health Safety-Net Hospital.
authors: Abdeen A, Olszewski N, Bemis K, Kain MS, Freccero DM, Tornetta P 3rd
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3284-e3292. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01301. Epub 2026 May 13.

Impact of an Orthopaedic-Driven Perioperative Protocol to Optimize Social and 
Medical Risk (SAFE) following Elective Total Joint Arthroplasty in a Health 
Safety-Net Hospital.

Abdeen A(1), Olszewski N, Bemis K, Kain MS, Freccero DM, Tornetta P 3rd.



BACKGROUND: Preoperative optimization of medical risk factors before total joint 
arthroplasty of the hip and knee improves outcomes. Arthroplasty programs in 
health safety-net hospitals have increased risk of complications because of 
increased medical complexity and disparities of social determinants of health. 
We propose a novel, orthopaedic team-driven perioperative optimization protocol 
to comprehensively and systematically address medical and social risk factors 
before total joint arthroplasty. We aim to evaluate the effect of optimizing 
medical and social risk factors on outcomes after hip and knee arthroplasty in a 
health safety-net hospital.
METHODS: A retrospective case-control series was done in a single, academic, 
tertiary-care, urban, safety-net hospital to compare complications (primary 
outcome) readmissions, length of stay (LOS), discharge disposition and 
escalation of care to intensive care unit (ICU), revision surgeries, and 
mortality (secondary outcomes) in patients who underwent hip or knee 
arthroplasty by a single surgeon before and after implementation of the 
optimization protocol. Follow-up duration was 12 months. Social determinants of 
health (SDOH) burden between groups were compared.
RESULTS: Of 808 primary total joint arthroplasty patients, 409 had surgery after 
the optimization protocol was implemented and 399 control subjects had surgery 
before implementation. Study patients had lower 90-day deep infection rate 
(0.24% vs 1%; P = 0.017) and 1-year deep infection rate (0.24 vs 2.01%; P = 
0.017) compared with control subjects, respectively. Study patients versus 
control subjects: LOS (3.0 vs 3.5 days, P = 0.012), discharge to skilled nursing 
facility (SNF) (11.0 vs 17.0%, P = 0.015), escalation to ICU care (0.25 vs 2.5%, 
P = 0.006), and 1-year mortality (0.24 vs 2.5%, P = 0.074), respectively. SDOH 
burden was similar between control and study groups.
CONCLUSION: Implementation of an orthopaedic-driven, standardized protocol 
designed to address modifiable medical and social risk factors before elective 
primary hip and knee arthroplasty was associated with reduced infection, LOS, 
discharge to SNF, and escalation of ICU care in a health safety-net hospital.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: The Influence of Peripheral Artery Disease on Postoperative Complications Following Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Ankle Fractures.
authors: Sontam TR, Tummala S, Mittal MM, Wukich DK
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3359-e3363. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01630. Epub 2026 Apr 21.

The Influence of Peripheral Artery Disease on Postoperative Complications 
Following Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Ankle Fractures.

Sontam TR(1), Tummala S, Mittal MM, Wukich DK.



BACKGROUND: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) has been associated with an 
increased risk of wound complications and surgical site infection following open 
reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) for ankle fractures. However, longer-term 
outcomes, including fracture healing, remain poorly characterized. This study 
evaluates the association between PAD and short- and long-term postoperative 
complications following ankle ORIF.
METHODS: The TriNetX Research Network was queried to identify patients who 
underwent isolated unimalleolar, bimalleolar, trimalleolar, or syndesmotic ORIF 
for ankle fractures. Patients were classified as having PAD if they had a 
documented diagnosis within 6 months before surgery, whereas patients without 
PAD served as controls. PAD and non-PAD cohorts were 1:1 propensity score 
matched for demographics and medical comorbidities. Postoperative complications 
were assessed at 90 days and 2 years.
RESULTS: After propensity matching, 2,159 patients were included in each cohort. 
At 90 days, patients with PAD had markedly higher rates of surgical site 
infection (5.5% vs 2.0%), wound disruption (10.2% vs 3.9%), lower extremity 
cellulitis (7.6% vs 2.1%), and acute osteomyelitis of the ankle or foot (3.1% vs 
0.6%) (all P < 0.001). At 2 years, PAD was associated with increased risks of 
nonunion (RR 3.07, 95% CI, 1.69 to 5.60), chronic osteomyelitis (RR 8.42, 95% 
CI, 4.64 to 15.27), implant infection (RR 3.19, 95% CI, 2.47 to 4.11), implant 
removal (RR 1.54, 95% CI, 1.32 to 1.81), and below-knee amputation (RR 10.5, 95% 
CI, 5.50 to 20.03) (all P ≤ 0.0001).
CONCLUSIONS: PAD is associated with markedly increased short- and long-term 
complications following ankle ORIF, including a sustained risk of impaired 
fracture healing. These findings underscore the importance of long-term risk 
stratification in patients with PAD undergoing ankle fracture fixation.

title: A pre-specified surgical-complexity index is associated with a graded increase in periprosthetic joint infection after total knee arthroplasty: a competing-risks analysis using coronal alignment as a negative control.
authors: Hoskins W, Gusho C, Rosser K, Lim M, Dunstall K, Vince KG
abstract:
1. J Bone Jt Infect. 2026 Nov 11;11(6):705-713. doi: 10.5194/jbji-11-705-2026. 
eCollection 2026.

A pre-specified surgical-complexity index is associated with a graded increase 
in periprosthetic joint infection after total knee arthroplasty: a 
competing-risks analysis using coronal alignment as a negative control.

Hoskins W(1)(2)(3), Gusho C(4), Rosser K(1), Lim M(1), Dunstall K(1), Vince 
KG(1).



Prediction of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) after total knee arthroplasty 
(TKA) relies almost wholly on host factors, and whether the operation itself 
carries infection risk independent of the patient is unknown. We analyzed 2920 
primary TKAs in 2350 patients from a single institution with national joint 
registry linkage, using death as a competing risk and coronal alignment as a 
negative-control exposure. A pre-specified surgical-complexity index counted 
five construct markers at the index operation: constraint, a tibial stem, a 
femoral stem, a previous implant and a pre-existing extra-articular deformity or 
fracture. Septic revision was the primary outcome and aseptic revision the 
control. Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models with patient-level clustering 
estimated complexity and, in the paired-radiograph subset, neutral-alignment 
effects on both outcomes. There were 51 septic and 104 aseptic revisions and 525 
deaths over a median follow-up of 7.4 years. Each additional complexity marker 
raised the subdistribution hazard of PJI (sHR 1.61, 95% CI 1.27-2.04) but not of

title: Local Bone Density of Preoperative CT: A Predictor of Clinically Significant Shortening and Varus Collapse of Well-Reduced Geriatric Intertrochanteric Hip Fractures.
authors: Kashyap J, Kuhn MZ, Kallakuri S, Moloney GB
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 11. doi: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-26-00061. Online
ahead  of print.

Local Bone Density of Preoperative CT: A Predictor of Clinically Significant 
Shortening and Varus Collapse of Well-Reduced Geriatric Intertrochanteric Hip 
Fractures.

Kashyap J(1), Kuhn MZ, Kallakuri S, Moloney GB.



INTRODUCTION: Intertrochanteric (IT) fractures are the most common geriatric hip 
fracture, with early fixation failure contributing to high morbidity and 
mortality. Lower bone density, as measured by Hounsfield units (HU) from CT 
scans, is predictive of various long bone fractures and fracture fixation 
failure, although its role in IT fractures is less well described. We aimed to 
assess the association between local bone density and radiographic outcomes 
after cephalomedullary nail (CMN) fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT 
fractures, hypothesizing that lower HU measurements are associated with 
increased rates of clinically significant shortening and varus collapse.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients older than 60 years with 
low-energy IT fractures treated with a long or short CMN between 2017 and 2024 
at a single institution. Fractures with varus malreduction or tip apex distance 
>25 mm were excluded. Radiographs were assessed postoperatively and at 6 to 
24-week follow-up to evaluate for shortening and change in the neck-shaft angle. 
Hounsfield unit measurements of the proximal femur were obtained from injury CT 
scans. Two-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, and multivariate logistic 
regression were used to analyze the relationship between HU and shortening/varus 
collapse.
RESULTS: Among 103 patients (74 women, 29 men; mean age 79.3 ± 9.8 years), the 
mean local bone density was 193.3 ± 63.4 HU. Patients with clinically 
significant shortening or varus collapse (n = 38) had significantly lower HU 
than those without (n = 65) (160.9 vs. 212.3 HU, P < 0.0001). HU was 
independently associated with shortening/varus collapse (OR 0.98, P < 0.01) and 
negatively correlated with magnitude of shortening (R2 = 0.091, P < 0.01). An 
exploratory threshold of 150 HU significantly predicted shortening.
CONCLUSIONS: Lower local bone density predicts shortening/varus collapse after 
CMN fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, despite optimization of 
modifiable surgical factors. An exploratory threshold of 150 HU may identify 
patients at risk of shortening within 24 weeks postoperatively.

title: A narrative review on the translational and clinical application of platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow concentrate and microfragmented adipose tissue for meniscal tears.
authors: Pattappa G, Müller N, Zellner J, Docheva D, Angele P
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 10. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70655.
Online  ahead of print.

A narrative review on the translational and clinical application of 
platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow concentrate and microfragmented adipose tissue 
for meniscal tears.

Pattappa G(1), Müller N(2), Zellner J(3), Docheva D(1), Angele P(2)(3)(4).



Meniscal tears are a common knee pathology with an annual incidence of 66 per 
100,000 patients and are associated with pain and an increased risk of 
osteoarthritis (OA). Orthobiological therapies have emerged as potential 
adjuncts to meniscal repair, but their clinical efficacy remains unclear. 
Minimally manipulated orthobiological therapies, including platelet-rich plasma 
(PRP), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) and microfragmented adipose 
tissue (MFAT), have primarily been investigated in OA therapies, with their use 
as adjuncts for meniscal tears subsequently investigated. This review evaluates 
the preclinical and clinical evidence for PRP, BMAC and MFAT in the treatment of 
meniscal tears. A literature search was performed to identify preclinical and 
clinical studies investigating PRP, BMAC and MFAT for meniscal tears. 
Methodology with respect to therapeutic approach and tear type was noted, whilst 
outcomes relating to meniscal healing and patient-reported clinical outcome 
measures were evaluated from the selected evidence. PRP was the most extensively 
studied approach amongst the orthobiologics reviewed, with heterogeneous 
findings in both preclinical and clinical studies. In general, PRP did not 
demonstrate significant differences in clinical outcome scores (Visual Analogue 
Scale, International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and 
Osteoarthritis Outcome Score or Lysholm) compared with suture-only controls in 
clinical studies, although one clinical study reported a lower re-rupture rate 
with PRP (14.6%) compared to suture-only (17%). Selected preclinical studies of 
BMAC indicated greater meniscal healing compared with PRP, although comparative 
clinical evidence remains limited. Clinical evidence for MFAT treatment of 
meniscal tears was restricted to case studies for degenerative meniscal tears in 
OA patients, with selected studies demonstrating improvements in 
patient-reported outcomes from baseline, although no preclinical animal studies 
using this approach were found. Heterogeneity in the application of these 
orthobiologics, tear type treated and surgical approach has led to inconsistent 
findings within the selected studies. Current evidence does not demonstrate 
consistent clinical superiority of PRP, BMAC or MFAT over standard meniscal 
treatments. PRP has the broadest but heterogeneous evidence base, whereas 
comparative clinical evidence for BMAC and MFAT remains limited. LEVEL OF 
EVIDENCE: N/A.

title: Chlorhexidine Gluconate and Hypersensitivity From 2-Octyl Cyanoacrylate Mesh Dressings.
authors: Aastroem K, Ossolinski G, Silverio L, Neuwirth AL, Cooper HJ, Shah RP
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3320-e3327. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-26-00078. Epub 2026 Jul 21.

Chlorhexidine Gluconate and Hypersensitivity From 2-Octyl Cyanoacrylate Mesh 
Dressings.

Aastroem K(1), Ossolinski G, Silverio L, Neuwirth AL, Cooper HJ, Shah RP.



BACKGROUND: Both 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh dressings and chlorhexidine 
gluconate are independently associated with hypersensitivity. Residual 
chlorhexidine antiseptic trapped under an impermeable mesh dressing may 
synergistically contribute to skin reactions. We hypothesized that an enhanced 
washing protocol before dressing application would reduce the incidence of 
hypersensitivity. We secondarily compared delayed wound healing, infection, and 
sensitization from prior exposure with mesh dressings.
METHODS: This retrospective study reviewed 214 hip and knee arthroplasty 
patients receiving 2% chlorhexidine gluconate/70% isopropyl alcohol skin paint 
and a 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh dressing. The standard wash protocol (n = 138) 
informally wiped the skin prep with saline. The enhanced wash protocol (n = 76) 
thoroughly removed the skin prep with an isopropyl alcohol-soaked sponge 
followed by a saline soaked sponge. The chart was reviewed for hypersensitivity, 
wound healing, infection, and prior exposure.
RESULTS: The enhanced wash protocol was associated with a notable decrease in 
the rate of hypersensitivity from 14.5 to 2.6% (OR 0.16, 95% CI, [0.04-0.70]). 
The two reactions in the enhanced protocol occurred immediately and both 
subsequently revealed a history of adhesive allergy. More folliculitis was 
observed in the enhanced group (3.9 vs. 0%, P = 0.04). No differences were 
observed in delayed wound healing, superficial infection, or deep infection ( P 
= 0.75, 0.53, and 1, respectively). Prior mesh exposure had no effect on 
hypersensitivity.
CONCLUSION: We observed that thorough removal of durable chlorhexidine paint was 
associated with a lower incidence of hypersensitivity after application of 
impermeable mesh dressings. The study findings support efforts to reduce 
chlorhexidine concentration on the skin before the application of dressings. In 
the absence of a prospective study, we recommend making this inexpensive and 
simple protocol change before application of a 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh 
dressing to surgical wounds.

title: Immediate Weight Bearing Is Safe Following Combined Extended Trochanteric Osteotomy and Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty.
authors: Abwini LZ, Tang A, Zeiman M, Andriani NT, Gillinov L, Shichman I, Schwarzkopf R, Liporace FA, Yoon RS
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3269-e3276. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01575. Epub 2026 May 11.

Immediate Weight Bearing Is Safe Following Combined Extended Trochanteric 
Osteotomy and Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty.

Abwini LZ(1), Tang A, Zeiman M, Andriani NT, Gillinov L, Shichman I, Schwarzkopf 
R, Liporace FA, Yoon RS.



INTRODUCTION: An extended trochanteric osteotomy (ETO) is used in complex cases 
to enhance access to the femoral canal and aid implant and cement removal during 
revision total hip arthroplasty (RTHA). However, there is no consensus regarding 
postoperative rehabilitation protocols. The aim of this study was to assess the 
efficacy and safety of immediate weight-bearing (WB) protocols in patients 
undergoing ETO during RTHA.
METHODS: A multicenter retrospective review was conducted at two academic 
medical centers between 2014 and 2021 to identify patients undergoing an ETO 
during RTHA with a minimum 1-year follow-up. Thirty-nine patients underwent an 
immediate WB protocol postoperatively. Union rates, ambulatory status, 90-day 
orthopaedic-related complications, revision surgeries, revisions, and Hip 
Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Joint Replacement (HOOS JR) scores 
were collected.
RESULTS: Fifty-three patients were included in the final analysis. The average 
follow-up time was 15.8 ± 20.4 months, with a mean age of 63.7 ± 11.5 years. 
Bony union was achieved in 46 patients (86.8%). The mean earliest time to union 
was 4.2 ± 5.4 months. Average HOOS JR scores significantly improved from 
preoperative to 1-year follow-up (mean 16.4 ± 4.1 vs 3.5 ± 4.2), P ≤ 0.000001). 
At the final follow-up, ambulatory status improved, with fewer patients kept as 
non-weight bearing (11 (21.6%) versus 7 (15.2%)). Two complications (3.8%) due 
to deep infection, 5 revision surgeries (9.4%), and 6 revisions (11.0%) were 
observed within 90 days.
CONCLUSION: Most patients who underwent ETO during RTHA and were placed on an 
immediate WB protocol achieved union at 4.2 months on average. HOOS JR scores 
improved as early as 2 weeks. More importantly, a greater proportion of patients 
experienced an improved ambulatory status at the final follow-up. These findings 
suggest that an immediate WB protocol-particularly WBAT-may be effective and 
safely implemented in patients undergoing an ETO during RTHA.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III retrospective cohort comparison study.

abstract:

Those with graft length of 25 mm or more inside the femoral tunnel were not at 
lower risk of graft tear in soccer players submitted to anatomical anterior 
cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Mónico JL(1), Andrade R(2), Mónico L(3), Silva JA(4), Linhares D(5), 
Monteiro-Soares M(6), Espregueira-Mendes J(7).



INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Anatomical anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) 
reconstruction can lead to shorter femoral tunnels, which can have decreased 
load capacity to failure. How much graft needs to be inside the femoral tunnel 
to allow proper graft integration and protect against graft tears remains 
unclear. The primary aim was to compare the rate of graft tear after ACL 
reconstruction in high-level soccer players between those with 25 mm or more of 
length of graft within the femoral tunnel (vs 20-24 mm).
METHODS: A total of 63 soccer players (mean age 22 ± 5.2 years, male-to-female 
ratio of 6:1) with a Tegner score ≥9 who underwent anatomical ACL reconstruction 
using the arthroscopic antero-medial technique with hamstrings autograft between 
January 2021 and May 2024 were included. The primary outcomes were the incidence 
of graft tear and the length of graft within the femoral tunnel. The secondary 
outcomes included graft diameter and femoral tunnel length. Patients were 
followed for 24 months to evaluate new knee injuries, graft tear, and 
return-to-sports (RTS) rates. RTS was defined as rejoining previous competitive 
sports.
RESULTS: Seven athletes (11.1%) suffered a graft tear. The overall RTS rate was 
71% (45/63, secondary outcome), while the new knee injury rate was 19.1% (12/63) 
(secondary outcome). Graft length within the femoral tunnel was 24.3 ± 2.3 mm 
(20-28 mm) and was not significantly different between those with and without 
graft tear (23.8 mm vs 24.4 mm, p = 0.08). Similarly, total femoral tunnel 
length (p = 0.47), concomitant knee injuries (p = 0.32) and graft diameter (p = 
0.67) were not statistically significantly different between those with and 
without graft tear.
CONCLUSIONS: The ACL graft length inside the femoral tunnel was not different 
between those with and without graft tear in a limited sample of 63 high-level 
soccer players undergoing anatomical ACL reconstruction with hamstrings 
autograft and followed for 2 years. Aiming for 25 mm or more of graft inside the 
femoral tunnel does not seem to provide an advantage in reducing the risk of 
graft tears as compared to 20-24 mm.

title: Minimally invasive two-incision bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft harvesting of the knee using a low-profile cutting guide: A current technique.
authors: Nguyen QD, Mai DT, Do DT, Nguyen VL, Mai DV, Dang TK, Quyen Nguyen QT
abstract:

Minimally invasive two-incision bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft harvesting 
of the knee using a low-profile cutting guide: A current technique.

Nguyen QD(1), Mai DT(2), Do DT(3), Nguyen VL(4), Mai DV(5), Dang TK(6), Quyen 
Nguyen QT(7).



The bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) graft is a reference autograft for anterior 
cruciate ligament reconstruction because of its consistent dimensions and early 
bone-to-bone healing. However, traditional harvesting through a long anterior 
incision is associated with donor-site morbidity, including anterior knee pain, 
sensory disturbance, and, rarely, patella fracture. This current technique 
describes a minimally invasive two-incision BPTB harvesting method using a 
low-profile cutting guide device. It is indicated for primary reconstruction in 
active patients who require reliable graft fixation. The key steps are careful 
dissection of the paratenon, stable fixation of a positioning guide with 
Kirschner wires, and advancement of a sliding tendon cutter along the fixed 
guide. This guided track standardizes the graft width at 10 mm and protects the 
tendon and paratenon. The depth of the patellar bone cut is limited to reduce 
the risk of fracture. In our early single-center experience, graft width was 
reproducible (10.0-10.2 mm), and there was no tendon transection or patella 
fracture. Arthroscopy confirmed preservation of the paratenon, and anterior knee 
pain and localized numbness were uncommon at short-term follow-up. The 
instruments, the step-by-step technique, and pearls and pitfalls are presented 
with an operative video. LEVEL 1: Knee. LEVEL 2: Anterior cruciate ligament 
reconstruction - autograft harvesting.

title: Effect of Mechanical Alignment on Clinically Significant Outcomes, Reoperation, and Failure After Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation of the Knee.

abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov 10:3635465261500856. doi: 10.1177/03635465261500856.

Effect of Mechanical Alignment on Clinically Significant Outcomes, Reoperation, 
and Failure After Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation of the Knee.

Sardesai KS(1), Ackermann J(1), Vega T(1), Kunze KN(1), Jesse JE(1), Alfonsi 
S(1), Caplan BE(1), Morgan JT(1), Friedman LR(1), Gilat R(2)(3), Yanke A(1), 
Chahla J(1), Cole BJ(1).



BACKGROUND: Identifying and addressing mechanical malalignment is an important 
component of treating symptomatic osteochondral defects with osteochondral 
allograft (OCA) transplantation. However, little is known about how malalignment 
influences short- to midterm outcomes after OCA transplantation.
PURPOSE: To evaluate whether mechanical alignment measurements including the 
hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle, lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA), medial proximal 
tibial angle (MPTA), and joint line convergence angle (JLCA) predict clinically 
significant outcome achievement, graft failure, and reoperation after OCA 
transplantation with or without concomitant realignment.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were collected preoperatively 
and at a minimum 2-year follow-up in patients receiving OCA from 2005 to 2023. 
PROMs included the International Knee Documentation Committee score and Knee 
injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score subscales. Clinically significant 
outcome thresholds were the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), 
substantial clinical benefit (SCB), and Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS). 
Preoperative full-length, weightbearing radiographs were used to measure the HKA 
angle, LDFA, MPTA, and JLCA. Multivariable logistic regression was used for 
clinically significant outcome achievement and all-cause reoperation; failure 
and arthroplasty were summarized descriptively because of the low number of 
events.
RESULTS: A total of 66 patients (mean age, 34.1 ± 11.5 years; mean body mass 
index, 27.8 ± 4.8 kg/m2; 50% female) met inclusion criteria. Mean alignment 
measurements were 1.8°± 4.0° for the HKA angle, 86.8°± 2.3° for the LDFA, 86.3°± 
2.3° for the MPTA, and 1.7°± 1.0° for the JLCA. Although PROMs improved at the 
final follow-up, no preoperative alignment measure was statistically associated 
with MCID, PASS, or SCB achievement or with all-cause reoperation (P > .05). In 
total, 25 (37.9%) patients underwent reoperation; graft survivorship was 93.9%, 
with 4 failures and 3 arthroplasty conversions. In an exploratory subanalysis, 
16 patients with an HKA angle >5° of varus or valgus (13 with concomitant 
realignment) did not have significantly different rates of reoperation (43.8% vs 
36.0%; P = .768) or graft failure (6.3% vs 6.0%; P > .999) compared to their 
remaining counterparts.
CONCLUSION: In this small, heterogeneous cohort, preoperative mechanical 
alignment measures were not statistically associated with clinically significant 
outcome achievement or all-cause reoperation after OCA transplantation. These 
hypothesis-generating findings do not establish the absence of an alignment 
effect or define a threshold for realignment because most patients with severe 
preoperative malalignment underwent concomitant realignment, which may have 
contributed to the favorable overall outcomes, and failure events were 
infrequent.

title: The Open Versus Closed Access Publication Advantage in Orthopaedic Surgery.
authors: Kothari SK, Nemirov D, Shamith S, Kothari NK, Ilyas AM
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3239-e3246. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00915. Epub 2026 May 13.

The Open Versus Closed Access Publication Advantage in Orthopaedic Surgery.

Kothari SK(1), Nemirov D, Shamith S, Kothari NK, Ilyas AM.



BACKGROUND: As scientific publishing has shifted to digital platforms, two 
primary article-publishing modalities have emerged: open access and closed 
access. Open access is freely accessible with an article processing charge (APC) 
paid by authors, whereas closed access lies behind paywalls, with low to no APC 
for authors. As the academic community increasingly relies on digital 
dissemination, it is critical to evaluate how these models influence research 
visibility and impact. This study compared open versus closed access randomized 
control trials (RCTs) across five prevalent orthopaedic conditions by analyzing 
attention scores, social media metrics, readership, and citations. The study 
hypothesis was that open access publications would have higher attention and 
readership, whereas closed access articles would yield more citations.
METHODS: A PubMed search was conducted in May 2025 to identify RCTs on rotator 
cuff tears, carpal tunnel syndrome, hip fractures, anterior cruciate ligament 
tears, and Achilles tendon ruptures. Altmetric Attention Scores, X mentions, 
Facebook mentions, news mentions, Mendeley readers, and Dimensions citations 
were collected for each article using the Altmetric Explorer database. A 
negative binomial regression, adjusted for time since publication, was used to 
compare metrics between open and closed access publications.
RESULTS: Of 1,223 articles studied, 53.8% of the articles were open access and 
46.2% were closed access. Open access articles had significantly higher 
Altmetric Attention Scores (44.1 ± 197 vs 17.2 ± 52.0), X mentions (32.2 ± 27.1 
vs 17.4 ± 38.4), Facebook mentions (1.2 ± 4.3 vs 1 ± 2.5), news mentions (4.1 ± 
25.2 vs 1.0 ± 7.2), number of Mendeley readers (136.6 ± 127.9 vs 113.4 ± 108), 
and, notably, number of Dimensions citations (36.8 ± 88.9 vs 30.1 ± 45.6) 
compared with closed access articles ( P < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Contrary to our initial hypothesis, open access articles had higher 
attention metrics and citation numbers when compared with closed access 
publications. These findings suggest that open access publishing not only 
enhances visibility and engagement but also may increase academic impact across 
multiple orthopaedic subspecialties.

defects in a skeletally immature porcine knee model.

INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the capitellum 
presents a clinical challenge in preadolescent and adolescent athletes. Although 
debridement is effective, residual defects remain a persistent concern, 
typically resulting in inferior fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage, 
despite the high intrinsic repair potential of cartilage in skeletally immature 
patients. Focused shock wave therapy (FSWT) shows promise in small animal models 
of osteochondral defects, but its efficacy in a clinically relevant, skeletally 
immature large animal model remains unknown. This study evaluated the effect of 
a single FSWT application on acute osteochondral defects intended to represent 
postdebridement tissue loss in a skeletally immature porcine knee model.
METHODS: Bilateral medial femoral condyle osteochondral defects (5-mm diameter, 
7-mm depth) were created in seven 6-week-old pigs. Right knees received a single 
FSWT application (2500 impulses, 0.20 mJ/mm2) directly to the defect immediately 
after its creation, and left knees served as untreated controls. At 6 weeks, 
evaluations included Goebel macroscopic and Niederauer histological scores, 
immunofluorescence analysis (SOX9, aggrecan, and COL2A1), and computed 
tomography to assess premature physeal closure.
RESULTS: There was no statistically significant difference in the median Goebel 
macroscopic score between the FSWT and control groups (5.5 [interquartile range 
{IQR}, 3.5, 7.8] vs. 8.5 [IQR, 4.0, 9.0], lower is better; P = 0.397). The 
median Niederauer histological score was statistically significantly higher in 
the FSWT group (14.0 [13.3, 14.7] vs. 13.0 [11.3, 13.5]; P = 0.042). 
Immunofluorescence showed that the median percentage of SOX9-positive cells was 
statistically significantly greater in the FSWT group (20.1% [12.4, 22.3] vs. 
11.6% [7.4, 18.4]; P = 0.018), as was the median aggrecan-positive 
immunoreactive fraction (15.2% [7.1, 18.5] vs. 7.1% [6.9, 10.7]; P = 0.028). The 
median COL2A1-positive immunoreactive fraction showed no statistically 
significant difference (4.0% [3.1, 7.8] vs. 2.8% [2.4, 4.9]; P = 0.499). No 
premature epiphyseal closure was observed at 6 weeks.
CONCLUSION: A single FSWT application improved the 6-week histological repair of 
an acute osteochondral defect in a skeletally immature porcine model. This 
improvement was accompanied by statistically significant increases in the 
percentage of SOX9-positive cells and the aggrecan-positive immunoreactive 
fraction. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of FSWT.

title: Comparison of computed tomography-based tibial torsion measurement techniques reveals significant technique-dependent differences.
authors: Benefelds M, Juen U, Kaiser P, Lindtner R, Kummann M, Mayr R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 9. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70672.
Online  ahead of print.

Comparison of computed tomography-based tibial torsion measurement techniques 
reveals significant technique-dependent differences.

Benefelds M(1), Juen U(2), Kaiser P(1)(3), Lindtner R(1), Kummann M(2), Mayr 
R(1).



PURPOSE: To compare commonly used computed tomography (CT)-based tibial torsion 
measurement discrepancies and evaluate their intra- and interobserver agreement, 
as measurement discrepancies between techniques have not been systematically 
assessed.
METHODS: CT scans from 20 adult patients were retrospectively analysed. Tibial 
torsion was calculated using two proximal reference axes (posterior tibial 
plateau tangent and tibial tuberosity axis) and four distal axes 
(transmalleolar, ankle joint, Jend and Waidelich). Three observers performed all 
measurements independently and repeated them after 8-12 weeks. Differences among 
techniques were assessed using repeated-measures analysis of variance with 
Bonferroni correction. Reliability was evaluated using intraclass correlation 
coefficients (ICCs).
RESULTS: All measurement techniques differed significantly (p < 0.05). Mean 
tibial torsion was 34.1° (standard deviation [SD] 8.6°) for the transmalleolar 
axis, 31.2° (SD 8.8°) for the ankle joint axis, 44.2° (SD 9.8°) for the Jend 
axis and 34.9° (SD 9.0°) for the Waidelich axis. Segmental values revealed a 
mean supratuberositary torsion of 26° (SD 6.7°) and a mean infratuberositary 
torsion of 7.9° (SD 8.8°) for the transmalleolar axis, 5.1° (SD 8.9°) for the 
ankle joint axis, 18.1° (SD 10.4°) for the Jend axis and 8.8° (SD 9.1°) for the 
Waidelich axis. All techniques showed excellent intra- and interobserver 
reliability (ICC > 0.89).
CONCLUSION: Tibial torsion values depended strongly on the measurement technique 
used. Technique-specific normative values are essential, and radiology reports 
should explicitly identify the technique applied. Clinicians must account for 
these systematic differences when interpreting torsion values and planning 
derotational osteotomies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study.

title: Does Specialty Matter? A Comparison of Early Postoperative Clinical Outcomes Following Lower Extremity Amputation Between Orthopaedic and Vascular Surgeons.
authors: Reddy S, Subramanian T, Lee W
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 15;34(22):e3342-e3358. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01375. Epub 2026 Apr 22.

Does Specialty Matter? A Comparison of Early Postoperative Clinical Outcomes 
Following Lower Extremity Amputation Between Orthopaedic and Vascular Surgeons.

Reddy S(1), Subramanian T, Lee W.



BACKGROUND: Lower extremity amputation (LEA) is performed by diverse 
specialties, including orthopaedic surgery and vascular surgery; whether 
outcomes differ by specialty remains uncertain. This study compared early 
postoperative outcomes after LEA performed by orthopaedic and vascular surgeons.
METHODS: Patients who underwent LEA surgeries were identified within the 
National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database. National Surgical 
Quality Improvement Program was queried for above-knee amputation, below-knee 
amputation, and foot amputations performed by orthopaedic or vascular surgeons. 
Patients were matched in a 1:1 ratio using propensity scores using a mixed 
exact/caliper approach. Primary outcomes were 30-day mortality, readmission, and 
revision surgery; secondary outcomes included cardiac, pulmonary, wound-related 
issues, and discharge disposition.
RESULTS: A total of 26,925 LEA cases were identified. After propensity matching, 
3,580 cases remained: orthopaedic surgery 1790 versus vascular surgery 1790, 
including 3,180 matched below-knee amputation, 806 matched above-knee 
amputation, and 334 matched foot amputations. Final cohorts had a similar 
distribution of demographic variables, indicating appropriate matching. 
Mortality of 4.0% versus 4.0%, readmission of 10.7% versus 11.7%, and revision 
surgery of 7.6 versus 8.3% were equivalent between orthopaedics and vascular 
surgery, respectively. The vascular cohort demonstrated higher rates of any 
postoperative complication: the sum of secondary outcomes (77.9% vs 70.4%; P < 
0.001), driven primarily by increased non-home discharge (69.7% vs 60.8%) and 
transfusion within 72 hours (19.5% vs 16.3%). When non-home discharge was 
removed, there was no difference in early postoperative complication (32.2% vs 
35.5%; P = 0.382). By contrast, the orthopaedic group had slightly higher rates 
of organ/space infection (4.1% vs 2.2%; P = 0.001) and postoperative pneumonia 
(3.8% vs 2.5%; P = 0.029), consistent with the higher proportion of 
contaminated/dirty wounds: 44.4% versus 36.0% and longer surgical duration: 79.5 
± 43.5 versus 68.3 ± 46.1 observed in this group.
CONCLUSIONS: The present analysis represents the first matched comparison of LEA 
outcomes by surgical specialty. When baseline patient risk is balanced, 
orthopaedic and vascular surgeons achieve comparable 30-day major outcomes: 
mortality, readmission, and revision surgery following LEA. Residual differences 
in complication profiles appear driven by clinical context, such as wound class, 
transfusion exposure, and rehabilitation needs, rather than by specialty itself.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.
